body.hook: Every person in Canada has rights that no government can simply take away, like freedom of expression and equality before the law. But rights come with responsibilities, because my rights end where they harm yours.

study.title: Rights and Responsibilities
study.question: What are our rights, and what responsibilities come with them?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Universal Declaration of Human Rights: adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 (now marked as Human Rights Day), with 30 articles.
Convention on the Rights of the Child: a UN treaty adopted in 1989; Canada ratified it in 1991. It includes rights to education, play, protection and having a say in decisions that affect you.
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982): fundamental freedoms (religion, expression, peaceful assembly, association) in section 2; democratic rights (voting); mobility rights; legal rights (life, liberty and security in section 7; fair treatment by police and courts); equality rights (section 15); official languages; minority language education rights. Section 1 allows "reasonable limits" that can be justified in a free and democratic society.
Alberta's Human Rights Act protects people from discrimination in areas like jobs, housing and services.
Rights and responsibilities pairs: freedom of expression ↔ not spreading hate or harassment; right to education ↔ respecting others' learning; equality ↔ treating others fairly.
Activity: match real-life situations to Charter sections, then write a responsibility for each right.
study.source: Summary from public sources: the UN, the Government of Canada and the Alberta Human Rights Commission.
steps: Learn about the UDHR and the Convention on the Rights of the Child
discussion: Which Charter right do you use most in daily life?
Why might free expression have limits?
How do children's rights apply at school?
study.product: Create a rights-and-responsibilities chart with five rights, their sources, examples and matching responsibilities.

examples.title: Responsibility

body.hook: Every post, comment, like and search leaves a trace. Online, the same ethics apply as face to face, but mistakes can spread faster, last longer and reach people you'll never meet.

study.title: Ethics Online
study.question: How do ethics apply to what I do online?
study.passage:
Key ideas (written for this lesson):
Digital footprint: posts, photos, comments, likes, searches and data apps collect. Screenshots mean deleting doesn't guarantee something is gone.
Privacy: protect personal information (full name with school, address, phone, passwords, location); check app settings; think before sharing others' information.
Consent: ask before posting photos or videos of others. Sharing someone's private messages or images without permission can hurt them badly and can break the law.
Misinformation: check before sharing: Who made this? What's the evidence? Do other reliable sources agree? Is it designed to make me angry?
Kindness: the "would I say it face to face?" test.
Activities: 1. Footprint audit: search for an imaginary student's posts (teacher-made profile); what impression do they give? 2. Scenarios (fictional): a friend's embarrassing video in a group chat; a viral post claiming a celebrity said something shocking; a game that asks for your location; someone asks for your password "just to help." For each: identify the ethical issue, the lenses, and a responsible choice. 3. Create a personal digital code of five rules.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: What impression did the imaginary profile give?
How can you tell if a post is misinformation?
Which rule in your code is most important to you?
study.product: Write a personal digital code of five rules, each with a reason linked to an ethical lens.

body.objective: Students will be able to analyze a global ethical issue.
body.iCan: I can analyze a global ethical issue.
successCriteria: I can explain what it means to be a global citizen
I can analyze a global ethical issue using lenses and stakeholders

body.hook: The T-shirt you're wearing may have been made by workers across the world. In 2013, the Rana Plaza factory building in Bangladesh collapsed, killing more than 1,100 garment workers. Global ethics asks what we owe to people we'll never meet.

vocabulary.definition: A person who sees themselves as part of a world community with shared responsibilities.
A moral problem that crosses borders, such as fair labour or climate.
All the steps and people involved in making and delivering a product.
A system aiming to give producers fair pay and safe conditions.
Depending on one another across countries.
Speaking up to support a cause.

study.title: Global Ethics
study.question: What responsibilities do we have to people around the world?
study.passage:
Case study and issues (written for this lesson from public sources):
Rana Plaza (24 April 2013): an eight-storey building near Dhaka, Bangladesh, housing garment factories collapsed after cracks were found the day before; more than 1,100 people died. Many global clothing brands sourced from factories there. Afterward, many brands signed an agreement to improve building and fire safety in Bangladesh factories.
Questions: Who is responsible? Factory owners, brands, governments, shoppers?
Other global issues to choose from: access to clean water; climate change and its unequal effects; child labour in cocoa or mining; vaccine and medicine access; refugees; e-waste shipped to other countries.
Analysis steps: stakeholders and how each is affected; apply the five lenses; identify actions at three levels: personal (buy less, buy second-hand, learn where products come from), community (school fundraiser, awareness campaign, letter to a company) and global (international agreements, organizations).
Product trace: pick an everyday item and trace its supply chain as far as you can; mark where ethical issues could arise.
study.source: Summary from public reporting on the Rana Plaza collapse; issues are widely discussed global topics.
steps: Propose personal, community and global actions
discussion: Who do you think was responsible for Rana Plaza, and why?
How are we connected to people who make our things?
Which action level feels most effective?
What does being a global citizen mean to you?
study.product: Analyze one global ethical issue with stakeholders, the five lenses and actions at personal, community and global levels.
